questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Eigenvalue that Corresponds to a Given Eigenvector
questions.problem:
Determine if $v=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 7 & 4\end{aligned}].$
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
questions.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 7 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}11 \\ 13\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

If $v$ is an eigenvector, then there must exist a real number $\lambda $ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ Hence, we have

$$
[\begin{aligned}11 \\ 13\end{aligned}]=\lambda [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

This leads to the following system of equations for $\lambda :$

$$
{\begin{aligned}11=3\lambda  \\ 13=-2\lambda \end{aligned}
$$

This system has no solution. Therefore, $v$ is not an eigenvector of $A.$

$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 5 & 7\end{aligned}].$

questions.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 5 & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

If $v$ is an eigenvector, then there must exist a real number $\lambda $ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ Hence, we have

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=\lambda [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

This leads to the following system of equations for $\lambda :$

$$
{\begin{aligned}2=2\lambda  \\ 3=-\lambda \end{aligned}
$$

This system has no solution. Therefore, $v$ is not an eigenvector of $A.$

$$

questions.problem: The eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ -k & -1\end{aligned}]$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =k-1$ is  $[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}].$ Determine the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =\lambda v \\ [\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ -k & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}] & =(k-1)[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-16 \\ -4k+4\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4k-4 \\ -4k+4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-16=4k-4, \\ -4k+4=-4k+4\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $k$ in the first equation, we get

$$
-12=4k\,⟹\,k=-3.
$$

The second equation is true for any value of $k.$

Therefore, the solution of the system is $k=-3.$

questions.problem:
An eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}]$ 
corresponding to an eigenvalue $\lambda =5k-4$ is $[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3k-1\end{aligned}].$ Determine the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =\lambda v \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3k-1\end{aligned}] & =(5k-4)[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3k-1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2+2(3k-1) \\ -10+8(3k-1)\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2(5k-4) \\ (5k-4)(3k-1)\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}6k \\ 24k-18\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}10k-8 \\ 15{k}^{2}-17k+4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}6k=10k-8 \\ 24k-18=15{k}^{2}-17k+4\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $k$ in the first equation, we get

$$
6k=10k-8\,⟹\,k=2.
$$

Now, substituting $k=2$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}24k-18 & =15{k}^{2}-17k+4 \\ 24\cdot 2-18 & =15\cdot {2}^{2}-17\cdot 2+4 \\ 30 & =30,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a true statement.

Therefore, the solution of the system is $k=2.$

questions.problem: An eigenvector of $D=[\begin{aligned}-8 & 10 \\ -7 & 11\end{aligned}]$ corresponding to an eigenvalue $\lambda =6$ is  $[\begin{aligned}c \\ 14\end{aligned}].$ Determine the value of $c.$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $D$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Dv=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Dv & =\lambda v \\ [\begin{aligned}-8 & 10 \\ -7 & 11\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}c \\ 14\end{aligned}] & =6[\begin{aligned}c \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-8c+140 \\ -7c+154\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}6c \\ 84\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-8c+140=6c \\ -7c+154=84\end{aligned}
$$

- Solving for $c$ in the first equation, we get

$$
-8c+140=6c\,⟹\,c=10.
$$

- Solving for $c$ in the second equation, we get

$$
-7c+154=84\,⟹\,c=10.
$$

Therefore, the solution of the system is $c=10.$

$$

$$

This gives us the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}5c+11=7c+7 \\ 13c-12=7c\end{aligned}
$$

- Solving for $c$ in the first equation, we get

$$
5c+11=7c+7\,⟹\,c=2.
$$

- Solving for $c$ in the second equation, we get

$$
13c-12=7c\,⟹\,c=2.
$$

Therefore, the solution of the system is $c=2.$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements About Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- If $v$ is an eigenvector of an invertible matrix $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =5$ then $v$ is also an eigenvector of the matrix ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to $\lambda =\frac{1}{5}.$
- An eigenvector of an invertible matrix $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =6$ is also an eigenvector of the inverse ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to the same eigenvalue $\lambda =6.$
- If $v$ is an eigenvector of a matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2,$ then $7v$ is also an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda =2.$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement is true. By the definition of an eigenvector, we have 

$$
Av=5v.
$$

 
Multiplying it by ${A}^{-1}$ from the left, we obtain 

$$
v=5{A}^{-1}v.
$$

Dividing both sides by $5$, we get 

$$
{A}^{-1}v=\frac{1}{5}v.
$$

 
So, $v$ is an eigenvector  of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\frac{1}{5}.$

**Note:** In general, an eigenvector of an invertible matrix $A$ that corresponds to an eigenvalue $\lambda $ is an eigenvector of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\frac{1}{\lambda }.$

- Statement II is false. According to the statement above, an eigenvector of $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =6$ is an eigenvector of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to $\lambda =\frac{1}{6}.$

- Statement III is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(7v)=7Av=7(2v)=2(7v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(7v)=2(7v),$ and $7v\ne 0,$ this implies that $7v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =2.$

**Note:** In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =1.$
- If $v$ is an eigenvector of a matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-7$ then $3v$ is also an eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda =-7.$
- $v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $0.$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =1\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =1v.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(3v)=3Av=3(-7v)=-7(3v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(3v)=-7(3v),$ and $3v\ne 0,$ this implies that $3v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =-7.$

**Note:** In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

- Statement III is false. An eigenvector must be a *non-zero* vector.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only".

$$

Multiplying it by ${A}^{-1}$ from the left, we obtain

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $2.$
- If $v$ is an eigenvector of a matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2,$ then $-v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda =-2.$
- $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $0.$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. We have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =2v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=2v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =2.$

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(-v)=-Av=-(2v)=2(-v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(-v)=2(-v),$ and $-v\ne 0,$ this implies that $-v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =2$ (but not $-2$).

**Note:** In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

- Statement III is true. We have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =0[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =0v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=0v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only".

\begin{aligned}A(10v)=10Av=10(5v)=5(10v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(10v)=5(10v),$ and $10v\ne 0,$ this implies that $10v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =5.$

**Note:** In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 18\end{aligned}] \\  & =6[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =6v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=6v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =6.$

- Statement III is true. We have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =4[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =4v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=4v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =4.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III".

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining the Value of an Unknown Given an Eigenvalue and Eigenvector of a Matrix
canonical_examples.problem: An eigenvector of ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14056271/assets/22ef70dcb0f7d3cba1c9d5514b40800144eb97edd004041ebb3516062a9e3e48.png) corresponding to an eigenvalue $\lambda=6c$ is  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14056271/assets/d1c2b9c36ec942a1c4113f1ff3a6221028f36c6ac4d109351ebab6bb48f358c4.png) Determine the value of $c.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $\mathbf{v}$ such that $A\mathbf{v}=\lambda \mathbf{v}.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =\lambda v \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2c\end{aligned}] & =6c[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2c\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2+2c \\ 1+4c\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}6c \\ 12{c}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2+2c=6c \\ 1+4c=12{c}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $c$ in the first equation, we get

$$
2+2c=6c \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad c = \dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, substituting $c=\dfrac{1}{2}$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1+4c & =12{c}^{2} \\ 1+4\cdot \frac{1}{2} & =12{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\ 3 & =3,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a true statement.

Therefore, the solutions of the system is $c=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14056271/assets/f35353367a395e7b3560aa6f7ef0da0936cefbced9e76d6d7d8f91426a7a1c9b.png) is an eigenvector of ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14056271/assets/0b4f33107845bf52d80802844bc6faaec6ab9f4bd159a87838497d2f6abe72d1.png) that corresponds to the eigenvalue $2.$

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14056271/assets/defb480233b4e48f90cb07fef771f2fdb62b6d7d5cb116393d74518eb3b37db8.png) is an eigenvector of ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14056271/assets/bb62b77da84018c07d4f3dfefc297684974db78b326bd0736469dc83572ae5b6.png) that corresponds to the eigenvalue $0.$

- If $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of a matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda = 5,$ then $2\mathbf{v}$ is also an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda = 5.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $\mathbf{v}$ such that $A\mathbf{v}=\lambda \mathbf{v}.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =2v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A\mathbf{v}=2 \mathbf{v},$ we conclude that $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda=2.$

- Statement II is false. An eigenvector must be a *non-zero* vector.

- Statement III is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(2v)=2Av=2(5v)=5(2v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(2\mathbf{v})=5( 2 \mathbf{v} ),$ and $2 \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0},$ this implies that $2 \mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda = 5.$

Therefore, the correct answer is, "I and III only."

**Note:** Statement III is true in the general case, too. In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.
